title: The royal way of the cross (II.12)
word: The royal way of the cross
hook: the cross is everywhere; carry it and it carries you
tomorrow: what if the voice you need is quieter than every notification?

segments.voice: Yesterday: many follow Jesus to the breaking of bread, few to the cup, and the cup is where friends are counted, in the quiet after. The line was to the cup.

Can carrying something heavy make it lighter? A backpack hanging off one shoulder drags all day. Cinch both straps, pull it in close, and the same weight rides easier. Nothing in the bag changed; the carrying did. Chapter twelve of book two makes a claim like that about the cross. It admits that deny yourself, take up your cross and follow sounds like a hard saying to many. Then it calls the road royal: the king's highway.
screen: `ONE STRAP, ALL DAY.` → `PULL IT IN CLOSE.` → `THE KING'S HIGHWAY.`

segments.voice: Ask the Imitation how to carry what can't be put down, and it answers: willingly. In the cross is salvation, the chapter says, in the cross is life, protection, strength of mind, joy of spirit. In the Latin it begins, in cruce salus. And the king walks the road first: he went ahead, the book says, carrying his own cross. You can't outrun it, either, because wherever you go, you bring yourself along. Then the line. Carry the cross willingly and it will carry you, and lead you where you long to go. Carry it unwillingly and you make it heavier, and you still have to carry it. That's the backpack. Same weight, different carrying. A neighbor tradition says something close about burdens. In the Qur'an, Pickthall's translation reads: "Allah tasketh not a soul beyond its scope." Both refuse to treat a burden as pointless, and both face it with God rather than alone. And here's one honest difference worth naming. The Imitation asks the reader to take up the cross, even to love it, because Christ carried his first. That same Qur'an verse closes with a prayer asking God not to lay on us more than we can bear. One posture picks the weight up and walks behind the king; the other trusts the measure and asks for mercy in it. Each in its own words.
screen: `IN THE CROSS IS LIFE.` · `CARRY IT, AND IT CARRIES YOU.` · `NOT BEYOND ITS SCOPE.` · `ONE HONEST DIFFERENCE.` · then, large: `THE ROYAL WAY.`

segments.voice: Pick up something with a little weight, a book or a bag, and hold it close against you with both arms. Breathe out the complaint and keep the weight; no need to lift much, and notice how it rides when it's held instead of dragged. If you pray, ask for the grace to carry yours willingly.
The royal way of the cross. The Imitation's name for the road Jesus walked first: the cross carried willingly, as a king's highway.

notes: Imitation II.12 paraphrased: to many this seems a hard saying, deny yourself, take up your cross and follow Jesus; in the cross is salvation, life, protection from enemies, strength of mind, joy of spirit; he went before carrying his cross; the cross is always ready and waits for you everywhere; you cannot escape it, for wherever you go you carry yourself; carry it willingly and it will carry you and lead you to the desired end; carry it unwillingly and you make a burden for yourself and must bear it still. Confirm each against the Latin.

Unity thread (v3 wisdom day): Qur'an 2:286 quoted from Pickthall (1930): 'Allah tasketh not a soul beyond its scope.' Confirm wording. The verse's closing prayer ('Our Lord! Impose not on us that which we have not the strength to bear!' in Pickthall, as remembered) is paraphrased, not quoted; confirm. The shared point (a burden faced with God, not treated as pointless) and the difference (the Imitation's call to take up and love the cross after Christ; the verse's trust in God's measure and its prayer for mercy in the load) describe these two texts only, ranking neither. A Muslim reviewer should confirm the framing.

Latin 'in cruce salus' quoted as the opening of the chapter's list; 'regia via' from the title 'De regia via sanctae crucis'. Confirm both and the pronunciations (ecclesiastical). 'The king's highway' is an interpretive gloss on 'royal way'. The chapter's harsher lines are left out on purpose.
II.12 is the last chapter of book two; the voice does not say so (claims rule). Confirm the book boundary in the Keeper's edition. Matthew 16:24 is paraphrased.
